intro: These patterns sit on one scale of pressure, from a gentle idea to an order. At the soft end are suggestions (〜たらどうですか, 〜といい, 〜ばいい); in the middle is advice with a warning behind it (〜たほうがいい); then a duty that comes from what is right (〜べきだ); and at the hard end are orders (〜なさい, the command form, 〜な). Pick by asking two things: how much pressure do I mean, and am I allowed to use it on this person?

skills.rule: Advice is た-form + ほうがいい ('you'd better do it'); warning is ない-form + ほうがいい ('you'd better not'), not なかったほうがいい.
skills.explain:
ほうがいい literally means 'the side of doing X is good': it compares two choices and says one is better, so there is a quiet warning behind it. If you don't follow the advice, something bad may happen. 傘を持っていったほうがいいよ suggests you will get wet otherwise.

For the positive, use the past tense: 行ったほうがいい, 食べたほうがいい, したほうがいい. The dictionary form (行くほうがいい) also exists but sounds like a general comparison; for advice to a person, use the た-form. For the negative, always use the plain non-past negative: 行かないほうがいい. For advice, the past negative なかったほうがいい is wrong.

This is firm advice. Use it with friends, family and juniors. Saying it to a teacher or boss sounds like you are lecturing them; use 〜たらいかがですか or rephrase the sentence instead.
patterns: [verb た-form] ほうがいい(です)
[verb ない-form] ほうがいい(です)

examples.jp: 今日[きょう]は早[はや]く寝[ね]{たほうがいい}ですよ。
examples.en: You'd better go to bed early today.

examples.jp: この水[みず]は飲[の]ま{ないほうがいい}です。
examples.en: You'd better not drink this water.

examples.jp: 雨[あめ]が降[ふ]りそうだから、傘[かさ]を持[も]っていっ{たほうがいい}よ。
examples.en: It looks like rain, so you should take an umbrella.

examples.jp: 熱[ねつ]があるなら、病院[びょういん]に行[い]っ{たほうがいい}。
examples.en: If you have a fever, you should go to the hospital.

examples.jp: 夜[よる]は一人[ひとり]で公園[こうえん]を歩[ある]か{ないほうがいい}と思[おも]います。
examples.en: I think it's better not to walk through the park alone at night.

contrast.note: てもいい only gives permission ('you may'); it does not push. 帰ってもいい = you can go home; 帰ったほうがいい = you should go home.
なければならない is an obligation from rules or necessity ('you have to'). ほうがいい is advice the listener may ignore at their own risk.
たらどうですか is a softer suggestion with no warning. ほうがいい implies there is a downside if you don't.

mistakes.bad: そこには行[い]か{なかったほうがいい}です。
mistakes.good: そこには行[い]か{ないほうがいい}です。
mistakes.note: The negative is always ないほうがいい; only the positive takes the past tense.

mistakes.bad: 今日[きょう]は早[はや]く寝[ね]る{のほうがいい}ですよ。
mistakes.good: 今日[きょう]は早[はや]く寝[ね]{たほうがいい}ですよ。
mistakes.note: ほう attaches directly to the verb, with no の in between.

skills.tip: Hear a hidden 'or else' after it? Then ほうがいい: positive in た, negative in ない.

skills.rule: 〜たらどうですか offers an idea, 〜といい recommends something (or hopes for it), and 〜ばいい says 'all you need to do is', usually answering どうすればいいですか.
skills.explain:
〜たらどうですか ('why don't you...?') puts an idea forward as a question: 先生に聞いたらどう? The polite version is 〜たらいかがですか. Even so, it can sound a little critical, as if the listener should have thought of it.

〜といい follows the dictionary form and recommends something that will work well: この店のラーメンを食べるといいよ. With ですね / なあ it becomes a wish about something the speaker cannot control: 明日晴れるといいですね ('I hope it's sunny tomorrow').

〜ばいい ('you just have to') gives the simplest way to reach a goal. It is the natural answer to どうすればいいですか / どうしたらいいですか: このボタンを押せばいいです. It also takes a wish form: もっと時間があればいいのに ('if only I had more time').

None of these carries the warning of ほうがいい.
patterns: [verb た-form] らどうですか / らいかがですか
[verb dictionary form] といい(ですよ / ですね)

examples.jp: 疲[つか]れているなら、少[すこ]し休[やす]ん{だらどうですか}。
examples.en: If you're tired, why don't you rest a little?

examples.jp: 明日[あした]、晴[は]れる{といい}ですね。
examples.en: I hope it's sunny tomorrow.

examples.jp: わからない言葉[ことば]は辞書[じしょ]で調[しら]べる{といい}ですよ。
examples.en: For words you don't know, it's a good idea to look them up in a dictionary.

examples.jp: 「どうすればいいですか。」「この紙[かみ]に名前[なまえ]を書[か]け{ばいい}です。」
examples.en: 'What should I do?' 'You just need to write your name on this sheet.'

examples.jp: 一度[いちど]、専門家[せんもんか]に相談[そうだん]してみ{たらいかがですか}。
examples.en: Why not try consulting a specialist?

contrast.note: ほうがいい warns ('or you'll regret it'). たらどう and といい simply offer an idea the listener can freely take or leave.
てもいい grants permission; it does not recommend. 休んでもいい = you're allowed to rest; 休んだらどう = why not rest?
てください asks the listener to do something. ばいい answers 'what do I need to do?' by naming the one step that is enough for their own goal.

mistakes.bad: 明日[あした]、晴[は]れ{たらどうですか}。
mistakes.good: 明日[あした]、晴[は]れる{といい}ですね。
mistakes.note: たらどう suggests an action to the listener; a hope about the weather takes といい.

mistakes.bad: 早[はや]く寝[ね]{たといい}ですよ。
mistakes.good: 早[はや]く寝[ね]る{といい}ですよ。
mistakes.note: といい takes the dictionary form; only たらどう uses the た-form.

mistakes.bad: 「どうすればいいですか。」「ここを{押[お]すばいい}です。」
mistakes.good: 「どうすればいいですか。」「ここを{押[お]せばいい}です。」
mistakes.note: ばいい needs the ば-form: 押す → 押せば, 食べる → 食べれば, する → すれば.

skills.tip: Question 'how do I?' → ばいい. Offering an idea → たらどう. Recommending or hoping → といい.

skills.rule: Stem + なさい is an order from someone in charge, the command form (行け, 食べろ, 来い) is a blunt order, and dictionary form + な (行くな) is a blunt 'don't'.
skills.explain:
〜なさい attaches to the ます-stem: 食べなさい, 早く寝なさい, 静かにしなさい. Parents use it to children and teachers to pupils, and exam questions use it: 次の質問に答えなさい. It is firm but not rude, because it comes from someone with authority.

The command form is blunt: godan verbs change the final -u to -e (行く→行け, 待つ→待て), ichidan verbs take ろ (食べろ, 見ろ), and the irregulars are しろ and 来い. You meet it in shouts (逃げろ!), sports, signs (止まれ), and reported orders (医者に休めと言われた).

The prohibition is the dictionary form + な: 触るな ('don't touch'), 入るな. Do not confuse it with stem + な (食べな), a soft casual command.

None of these should be said to superiors or strangers; use 〜てください / 〜ないでください.
patterns: [command form]: 行け / 食べろ / しろ / 来い

examples.jp: もう九時[くじ]よ。早[はや]く寝[ね]{なさい}。
examples.en: It's already nine. Go to bed now.

examples.jp: 次[つぎ]の文[ぶん]を読[よ]んで、質問[しつもん]に答[こた]え{なさい}。
examples.en: Read the following passage and answer the questions.

examples.jp: 危[あぶ]ない！{逃[に]げろ}！
examples.en: Look out! Run!

examples.jp: この線[せん]から中[なか]に{入[はい]るな}。
examples.en: Do not go beyond this line.

examples.jp: 医者[いしゃ]に一週間[いっしゅうかん]{休[やす]め}と言[い]われました。
examples.en: The doctor told me to rest for a week.

contrast.note: てください is a polite request anyone can use; なさい and the command form assume authority over the listener.
ましょう invites ('let's') and includes the speaker. なさい orders only the listener.
てもいい leaves the choice to the listener; a command removes it.

mistakes.bad: 先生[せんせい]、ここに座[すわ]り{なさい}。
mistakes.good: 先生[せんせい]、ここに座[すわ]っ{てください}。
mistakes.note: なさい is spoken downward; to a teacher it is rude.
来る is irregular: its command form is 来い.

mistakes.bad: ここで写真[しゃしん]を{撮[と]らないな}。
mistakes.good: ここで写真[しゃしん]を{撮[と]るな}。
mistakes.note: The prohibition な attaches to the positive dictionary form.

skills.tip: Parent or teacher → なさい. Shout or sign → command form. Shouted 'don't' → dictionary form + な.

skills.rule: Dictionary form + べきだ says what someone ought to do because it is right; the negative is 〜べきではない, never 〜ないべきだ.
skills.explain:
べき expresses a duty based on morality, common sense or the speaker's principles: 約束は守るべきだ ('promises should be kept'). It is stronger and more judging than ほうがいい, which is practical advice, and it is not a rule imposed from outside (that is なければならない).

It attaches to the dictionary form. With する, both するべき and すべき are used; すべき is a little more formal. Before a noun it becomes べき: 読むべき本 ('a book you ought to read').

The negative goes on べき, not on the verb: 言うべきではない ('you shouldn't say it'). In the past, 〜べきだった expresses regret: もっと勉強するべきだった ('I should have studied more').

Said to someone's face, especially a superior, べきだ sounds like a lecture. It suits opinions, writing, and talking about yourself or people in general.
patterns: [verb dictionary form] べきだ / べきです
[verb dictionary form] べきではない

examples.jp: 約束[やくそく]は守[まも]る{べきだ}。
examples.en: Promises should be kept.

examples.jp: 人[ひと]の悪口[わるぐち]を言[い]う{べきではない}。
examples.en: You shouldn't speak ill of others.

examples.jp: 学生[がくせい]のうちに、いろいろな国[くに]へ行[い]く{べきです}。
examples.en: You ought to visit many countries while you're a student.

examples.jp: あの時[とき]、本当[ほんとう]のことを話[はな]す{べきだった}。
examples.en: I should have told the truth back then.

examples.jp: これは大人[おとな]が読[よ]む{べき}本[ほん]だと思[おも]います。
examples.en: I think this is a book adults ought to read.

contrast.note: はず is an expectation ('is supposed to, should be'): 彼はもう着いたはずだ = he should have arrived by now. べき is about duty, not likelihood.
つもり is the speaker's own plan ('intend to'). べき is a judgement of what is right, whether or not anyone plans to do it.
わけ explains a reason or conclusion ('that's why'). It never expresses duty.

mistakes.bad: そんなことは言[い]わない{べき}だ。
mistakes.good: そんなことは言[い]う{べきではない}。
mistakes.note: Put the negative on べき: べきではない.

mistakes.bad: 新幹線[しんかんせん]で来[く]るから、彼[かれ]は三時[さんじ]に着[つ]く{べき}です。
mistakes.good: 新幹線[しんかんせん]で来[く]るから、彼[かれ]は三時[さんじ]に着[つ]く{はず}です。
mistakes.note: Arriving at three because he is on the bullet train is an expectation, not a moral duty: はず.

skills.tip: Could you say 'it's the right thing to do'? Then べき. Negative? べきではない.
